items.prompt: What does a hash function produce from its input?
choices: A fixed-size fingerprint of the input
A reversible encrypted copy of the input
A random key chosen for the user
A smaller file that can be unpacked later
items.explanation: A hash maps any input to a fixed-size fingerprint. It is not an encrypted copy and cannot be unpacked.

items.prompt: You hash the same file twice, once on each of two computers. What do you expect?
choices: Different outputs, since hashing is random
Outputs that differ by a few bits
Outputs that depend on the clock time
The same output on both computers
items.explanation: Hashes are deterministic: same bytes, same fingerprint, on any machine.

items.prompt: SHA-256 is given a one-word input and a ten-gigabyte file. How long are the two outputs?
choices: The file output is far longer than the word output
Both are exactly 256 bits long
The word output is much shorter than 256 bits
Both match their input sizes
items.explanation: Output length is fixed by the function, not by the input.

items.prompt: What does the avalanche effect describe?
choices: A longer input always produces a longer fingerprint
The output slowly grows as files get hashed
A tiny input change scrambles the whole output
Two similar inputs share the start of their hashes
items.explanation: Avalanche means a small input change flips about half the output bits, unpredictably.

items.prompt: The hash you compute differs from the published one. What does that tell you?
choices: Your computer hashed it too slowly
Your file is not the published file
The hash needs one more round
The file is within tolerance of the original
items.explanation: Any difference in the hashes means the bytes differ. There is no tolerance.

items.prompt: Why compare two hashes instead of two whole files?
choices: Hashing a file makes the file itself smaller
A hash hides the file contents from any reader
Whole files cannot be compared by any program
Two short strings are far cheaper to compare
items.explanation: The fingerprint is short, so one comparison stands in for a full byte-by-byte check.

items.prompt: Can you recover the original file from its hash?
choices: No, going backwards is not practical
Yes, by running the hash in reverse
Yes, if the file is small enough
Yes, but only with the author's password
items.explanation: Hashing is one-way: easy forward, impractical backward.

items.prompt: Which of these changes the hash of a file?
choices: Hashing it again on the following day
Hashing it on a much faster computer
Changing a single letter inside the file
Hashing it while in a different country
items.explanation: Only the input bytes matter. Time, hardware and place do not.

items.prompt: A simple checksum adds up byte values, so AB and BA both give 131. What does that show?
choices: It shows the checksum has a strong avalanche effect on any edit
It shows input order cannot matter to any real hash function
It shows fixed-length output alone makes tampering detectable
It lacks collision resistance, so matching inputs can be forged
items.explanation: Different inputs sharing an output is a collision, and a function this easy to collide cannot resist a tamperer.
items.reference:
A hash is a fingerprint, not a copy
same input: same fingerprint, every time
any size in: one fixed size out
one letter changed: unrelated fingerprint
fingerprint back to input: no practical way
Why: the fingerprint is fixed-size, repeatable and scrambled by any change, so exact equality is the only meaningful check.
items.learnMore:
Fingerprints and avalanche

A hash maps any input to a fixed-size output that is the same every time and changes completely when the input changes even slightly. That makes comparing two short strings a reliable stand-in for comparing two whole files.

Common mistake

Thinking a close-looking hash means a close-looking file. No such closeness exists: any change scrambles about half the bits.
items.reflection: Think of another everyday situation where a short stamp stands in for something large (a receipt, a serial number, a seal). What would it take for someone to forge the stamp without anyone noticing?

items.prompt: Two inputs differ by one bit, and their 256-bit hashes agree on 200 bits. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Avalanche is failing, so this is not a sound hash
The files are nearly identical, so this is expected
Sharing more bits makes a hash stronger at integrity
Only the last 56 bits matter for integrity checks
items.explanation: A sound hash would disagree on about half of the bits. Sharing most of them breaks avalanche.

items.prompt: A site publishes a file and its hash on the same page. What is the weakness?
choices: The hash is too short to compare reliably by hand
Browsers silently hash the file twice before saving it
Whoever controls the page can swap both file and hash
The published hash changes each time the page is viewed
items.explanation: Matching hashes prove the file equals what the hash came from, not that the hash is trustworthy. It must come from a separate trusted channel.

items.prompt: The same bytes hash to a different value on every run. What is true about this system?
choices: It is normal because good hashes add fresh randomness each run
It is not deterministic, so it is unfit for any integrity check
It is stronger because outputs are harder for others to compare
It is fine because only the output length needs to stay stable
items.explanation: Integrity checks compare a stored fingerprint with a fresh one. Without determinism there is nothing to compare.

items.prompt: What is a hash collision?
choices: One input that gives two different hashes
A hash that is longer than the input it came from
Two different inputs that give the same hash
A hash computed on two separate machines at once
items.explanation: A collision is two distinct inputs mapping to one output.

items.prompt: What is a preimage of a given hash?
choices: An input that produces that hash
The hash of the empty input
The hash computed twice in a row
The first bit of the hash
items.explanation: A preimage is an input that hashes to the target value.

items.prompt: 100 objects go into 10 boxes. What must be true?
choices: Every box holds exactly ten objects
Every box holds at least one object
No box holds more than five objects
Some box holds more than one object
items.explanation: By the pigeonhole principle, more objects than boxes forces sharing.

items.prompt: Do collisions exist for SHA-256?
choices: No, SHA-256 never repeats an output
Yes, since inputs outnumber outputs
Only for inputs shorter than 256 bits
Only after the year 2030
items.explanation: Unlimited inputs and a fixed output space force collisions to exist somewhere.

items.prompt: What does collision resistance mean?
choices: No two inputs can ever share a hash value
Hashes can be reversed given enough patient effort
Finding a collision on purpose is infeasible
Hashes never change when moved between machines
items.explanation: Resistance is about cost, not about collisions being impossible.

items.prompt: Why are MD5 and SHA-1 called broken for collisions?
choices: They produce outputs of different lengths each run
Collisions can be found faster than brute force
They stopped giving the same output twice
They can no longer hash files above a certain size
items.explanation: A hash is broken when collisions are found faster than the generic bound.

items.prompt: A hash has k possible outputs. About how many tries until a collision is likely?
choices: About k tries, one per output
About k squared
About one try per input bit
About the square root of k
items.explanation: The birthday effect makes collisions likely after about the square root of k tries.

items.prompt: What does preimage resistance protect against?
choices: Recovering an input from only its hash
Two different inputs that share the same hash
Hashing being slow on very large files
Output length changing between two runs
items.explanation: Preimage resistance means a hash alone should not give back a matching input.

items.prompt: A hash has 2^40 possible outputs. About how many tries make a collision likely?
choices: About 2^40
About 2^20
About 2^80
About 2^10
items.explanation: The birthday effect needs about the square root of the output space: the square root of 2^40 is 2^20.
items.reference:
Collision vs preimage
preimage: given a hash, find any input for it
collision: find two inputs with the same hash
collisions must exist: more inputs than outputs
resistance: finding one on purpose is infeasible
Why: collisions exist by counting, and collision resistance means locating one costs about the square root of the output space.
items.learnMore:
Collisions and preimages

Because inputs are unlimited and outputs are not, collisions exist. A hash stays useful as long as finding one takes unreachable effort. The birthday effect makes collisions cost about the square root of the output space, so an n-bit hash gives about n/2 bits of collision resistance.

Common mistake

Treating "collisions exist" as "the hash is broken". It is broken only when collisions can be found faster than the generic bound.
items.reflection: Think of a naming or numbering scheme you use (usernames, tracking numbers, seats). At what size would two different things start sharing a name by accident?

items.prompt: A colleague says collisions must exist for SHA-256, so it is unsafe. What is the flaw?

SHA-256 is designed so that no collisions exist at all
Pigeonhole only applies to hashes with short outputs
Existing is fine; finding one on purpose is infeasible
items.explanation: Collisions exist by counting, but safety depends on the cost of locating one.

items.prompt: An attacker may choose both documents freely and wants any pair that hashes the same. Which property is this and why is it easier than matching a given hash?
choices: Collision resistance; any pair counts, so birthday math helps
Preimage resistance; any pair counts, so the birthday effect helps
Collision resistance; a fixed target makes the search shorter
Preimage resistance; a fixed target halves the whole search space
items.explanation: With free choice the attacker needs only a repeat anywhere, which costs about the square root. Matching a fixed hash does not get that discount.

items.prompt: A service truncates SHA-256 to 32 bits to detect duplicate uploads among 200,000 files. What is the risk?
choices: None, since 200,000 is far below the 2^32 output count
Only a determined attacker could ever cause a collision
Likely: 32 bits means about 65,000 tries to a collision
Truncation turns every file's hash into the same value
items.explanation: A 32-bit output reaches a collision after about 2^16, roughly 65,000 tries, which is below 200,000 files.

items.prompt: What is a KDF in this unit?
choices: A quick hash chosen for verifying large files
A tool that compresses passwords before storage
A deliberately slow, tunable hash for passwords
A master key that unlocks the entire database
items.explanation: A key derivation function is built to be slow and adjustable.

items.prompt: Why not store passwords with a fast hash?
choices: Fast hashes cannot be stored
Attackers could guess much faster
Fast hashes are always reversible
Fast hashes produce longer outputs
items.explanation: The faster the hash, the cheaper each guess.

items.prompt: What is an offline attack?
choices: Guessing through the live login page with lockouts
Guessing while the server is unplugged from power
Guessing on paper without using a computer at all
Guessing against a stolen copy with no rate limit
items.explanation: Offline means the attacker holds the data and the website cannot slow them down.

items.prompt: Is a fast hash good for checking downloaded files?
choices: Yes, quick hashing of many files is useful
No, every hash must be slowed down on purpose
No, fast hashes cannot detect any file changes
Only when a per-file salt has been added
items.explanation: Nobody is guessing secrets in a file check, so speed is a benefit.

items.prompt: Who pays a KDF's cost setting?
choices: Only the attacker
Only the owner of the server hardware
Every login and each attacker guess
Only users who have forgotten their password
items.explanation: The same cost applies to honest logins and to guesses.

items.prompt: What does memory hardness require?
choices: A large block of memory for each hash
A much faster processor in the server
A longer password from every single user
A second encrypted copy of the database
items.explanation: Needing memory per hash makes massive parallel guessing expensive.

items.prompt: Which of these is built to be slow for passwords?
choices: CRC-32
SHA-256
Adler32
scrypt
items.explanation: scrypt is a KDF designed with adjustable time and memory cost.

items.prompt: A KDF takes 50 ms per hash. How does a user feel one login?
choices: A bit annoying
Barely noticeable
Slower than a minute
Impossible to finish
items.explanation: 50 ms is a fraction of a second, invisible for one login.

items.prompt: Two databases are stolen, one hashed with plain SHA-256 and one with a tuned KDF. What differs most?
choices: Whether the password can be read directly
The cost per guess the attacker must pay
The length of the stored hash
Whether the site is online
items.explanation: Both store fingerprints, but the KDF makes each guess far more expensive.
items.reference:
Same word, opposite jobs
file check: one hash, speed is good
password theft: billions of guesses, speed helps the attacker
KDF: slow on purpose, cost is tunable
cost paid: once per login, once per guess
Why: offline guessing multiplies the per-hash cost by the number of guesses, so a slow hash punishes the attacker far more than one honest login.
items.learnMore:
Why password hashes are slow

An attacker with a stolen database guesses offline with no lockout. A fast hash makes each guess cheap. A KDF adds time cost and memory cost so each guess is expensive, while one real login barely notices.

Common mistake

Believing "hashed" is a single security level. A fast hash and a slow KDF are both hashed and protect very differently.
items.reflection: Think of a lock or gate where being slow to open is a feature (a bank vault time lock, a cooling-off period). Who pays the delay, and who is it meant to deter?

items.prompt: A site rate-limits its login page. Why does that not protect a stolen hash file?
choices: Rate limits are applied only to successful logins
Hash files are designed to bypass any rate limit
Rate limits slow down honest users and nobody else
Offline guessing never goes through the login page
items.explanation: The attacker guesses on their own hardware, outside the site's controls.

items.prompt: A team doubles its KDF cost setting. What is the effect?

It doubles the cost paid by the attacker only
It doubles the cost paid by honest logins only
It doubles the stored length of each password hash
items.explanation: The cost applies equally, so the attacker's total grows in proportion, and so does each user's wait.

items.prompt: A team switches their file-checksum job to scrypt for "extra security". What happens?
choices: It becomes much safer against tampering with the files
It becomes faster because scrypt is better optimised
It only gets slower; nobody is guessing file contents
It now only detects changes above a certain size
items.explanation: Integrity checks have no offline guessing threat, so slowness is pure cost.

items.prompt: What is a salt?
choices: A random value stored beside every user's hash
A secret key that only the server operator knows
A second password the user types at each login
A compression step performed before the hashing
items.explanation: A salt is random, per user, and stored beside the hash.

items.prompt: Does a salt have to be secret?
choices: Yes, it must be hidden from everyone
Yes, it must be a user's birthday
No, it can be stored in the open
Yes, but only for admin accounts
items.explanation: The salt's job does not rely on secrecy.

items.prompt: Two users pick the same password and both have salts. What do the stored hashes look like?
choices: Different from each other
The same for both of them
Left empty for both users
Each equal to the salt value
items.explanation: Different salts produce different hashes from the same password.

items.prompt: Should every user get the same salt?
choices: Yes, a single site-wide salt is the best
Yes, as long as the salt is kept very short
No, it must equal the username
No, each user should get their own
items.explanation: A shared salt keeps the shared-work problem alive.

items.prompt: What does a salt prevent?
choices: Users from forgetting their own passwords
One precomputed table cracking every account
The database from being stolen in a breach
Users from typing their password a second time
items.explanation: A table built for one salt does not fit another salt.

items.prompt: How is the salt used when hashing a password?
choices: It is appended to the hash after the hash is stored
It replaces the password before the KDF is run
It is mixed into the KDF input with the password
It is sent to the user's browser to be used as a key
items.explanation: The KDF takes both password and salt as input.

items.prompt: With no salt, two users share a password. What shows up in a stolen database?
choices: Different hashes
Identical stored hashes
Empty fields
Encrypted copies of the password
items.explanation: Same input and same function give the same output.

items.prompt: Does a salt make one targeted guess slower?
choices: Yes, by a factor of two
Yes, by the length of the salt
Yes, it adds a lockout
No, the KDF cost does that
items.explanation: A salt adds no per-guess work. It only stops shared work.

items.prompt: A system salts passwords but hashes with plain fast SHA-256. What remains weak?
choices: Identical passwords still give identical hashes
Precomputed tables work on all accounts
Each single guess is still cheap to try
The salt can be used to log in
items.explanation: The salt fixes shared work, but only a slow KDF makes each guess expensive.
items.reference:
What a salt changes
no salt: same password gives same hash for everyone
salt: random per user, stored beside the hash
effect: one precomputed table no longer fits all
not changed: the cost of one targeted guess
Why: a salt removes shared work between accounts, while the KDF cost sets the price of each guess.
items.learnMore:
Salts

A salt is a random per-user value stored next to the hash and mixed into the KDF. It is not secret. It stops identical passwords from producing identical hashes and stops one precomputed table from working on every account.

Common mistake

Thinking the salt must be hidden, or that it slows down one targeted guess. It does neither; the KDF cost does the slowing.
items.reflection: Think of a shared resource where giving each person a unique mark stops one trick from working on everyone at once (unique keys, unique serials). What stops a single master trick?

items.prompt: A leaked table shows many users with the same hash. What does that suggest?
choices: Each user was given the same salt by design
No per-user salt, so they share a password
Their passwords are all unusually strong ones
The KDF cost setting was far too high here
items.explanation: With a proper per-user salt, equal passwords would not give equal hashes.

items.explanation: A single shared salt acts like no salt at all as far as sharing is concerned.

items.prompt: Write msToSeconds(ms) that converts milliseconds to seconds.
items.explanation: There are 1000 milliseconds in a second, so divide by 1000.

items.prompt: Write guessesPerSecond(loginMs) giving how many hashes one core completes per second.
items.explanation: One second holds 1000 ms; each hash takes loginMs of them.

items.prompt: Write totalMs(loginMs, guesses) giving the time to run that many guesses one after another.
items.explanation: Each guess takes loginMs, so the total is the product.

items.prompt: Write msToDays(ms) that converts milliseconds to days.
items.explanation: A day has 24 x 60 x 60 x 1000 = 86,400,000 milliseconds.

items.prompt: Write doubleCost(ms) returning the per-hash time after raising the cost setting one step (cost doubles).
items.explanation: One step in the demo's model doubles the time.

items.prompt: Write costAfterSteps(baseMs, steps) giving per-hash time after that many doubling steps.
items.explanation: Each step doubles the time, so steps steps multiply by 2 to the power of steps.

items.prompt: Write isFastEnough(loginMs, budgetMs) returning true when a login fits within the budget.
items.explanation: A login fits the budget when it takes no more than the budget.

items.prompt: Write slowdown(oldMs, newMs) giving how many times slower the new setting is.
items.explanation: The ratio of new time to old time is the slowdown factor.

items.prompt: Write attackDays(loginMs, guesses): days one core needs to try that many guesses at loginMs each.
items.explanation: Total milliseconds is loginMs times guesses; dividing by milliseconds per day gives days.
items.reference:
Cost setting arithmetic
days = (ms per hash x guesses) / 86,400,000
2^10: 3.7 ms, 2^14: 50.1 ms (one machine)
1 billion guesses on one core: about 43 to 580 days
real attackers use many cores: divide the days
Why: the same per-hash cost is paid once by a user and billions of times by an attacker, so small waits become large campaigns.
items.learnMore:
Tuning a KDF

Raise the cost until one login is still comfortably fast. Total attacker time is the per-hash time times the number of guesses, divided by how many guesses run in parallel. Store the cost beside each hash and upgrade it at the next login.

Common mistake

Quoting an attacker's time for a single core as if it were a safe guarantee. Parallel hardware divides it.
items.reflection: Think of a deterrent that costs each honest person a little but each abuser a lot (a tollbooth, a fee per message). Where does it stop being worth the honest cost?

items.prompt: Write attackDaysParallel(loginMs, guesses, cores): the same total when work is split evenly across cores.
items.explanation: More cores divide the elapsed time, which is why a single-core figure is not a guarantee.

items.prompt: Write stepsToReach(baseMs, targetMs): the fewest doubling steps until per-hash time is at least targetMs.
items.explanation: Keep doubling until the time reaches the target. Zero steps are needed if the start already meets it.

items.prompt: Write bestCost(baseMs, budgetMs): the largest number of doubling steps whose per-hash time is still within the budget, or -1 if even zero steps is too slow.
items.explanation: Start from zero steps if the base fits at all, then take one more doubling while it still fits the budget.
